targets.from: judgement values from the drafter's reading of the sources and knowledge of the species (2026-11-10), no photographs measured; to be replaced by photo measurements: a dense, rounded, many-branched shrub about as wide as tall, its erect branches tipped in summer by upright cone-shaped clusters of small white flowers that dry brown; grey-green, finely divided, fern-like leaves, partly held brown through the winter

description: A dense, aromatic shrub one to three metres tall, its many erect branches covered in small grey-green leaves divided like tiny fern fronds, sticky and sweet-smelling when touched. In summer each branch ends in an upright, cone-shaped spray of small white rose-like flowers. At the Grand Canyon it grows on dry, rocky ground in the pinyon-juniper woodland along the rims and on the ledges and slopes of the canyon just below them.

season_notes.winter: Some leaves hang on, brown and curled, among bare grey-brown stems and last year's dry flower stalks.
season_notes.spring: New fern-like leaves unfold, sticky and fragrant; spring azure butterflies lay their eggs on it.
season_notes.summer: Upright spires of white flowers open from July at the branch tips.
season_notes.fall: Flowering goes on into fall in Arizona; the spent flower clusters dry to rusty brown and hold small seed pods.

range.where: dry, rocky ground in the pinyon-juniper woodland along the South and North Rims and on the bedrock ledges and talus just below the rims; across the Great Basin and Colorado Plateau, from Oregon and Idaho to California, Arizona and New Mexico

notes: Mountain misery (the template) is the library's fern-leaved Rosaceae shrub (pinnate_compound leaves), but it is an evergreen carpet under half a metre in the Sierra; the card makes fernbush a dense upright shrub of 1-2.5 m (FEIS: 1-3 m; NPS Grand Canyon shrubs page: 3-10 ft, densely branched), with leaves 1-8 cm, twice pinnately compound, like minute fern fronds (FEIS; NPS: 1-4 in, sticky glands, a pleasant aroma; Wikipedia: hairy and sticky), so leaf_size_m 0.05. Flowers: white, rose-like (Wikipedia), in panicles or racemes (FEIS), a cone-shaped cluster (NPS), hence the candle form; FEIS gives July-November bloom in Arizona and June-August in California, and the card draws July-September for the rims, which is the drafter's reading. The fruit is a small dry follicle (FEIS), not drawn. Deciduous or semi-evergreen: no source read says, so the card is deciduous with about a third of its leaves held through winter, the drafter's judgement. Habitat: dry rocky sites, gravel to clay-loam, limestone soils in Nevada, pinyon-juniper woodland in Arizona (FEIS); its placing on the South Rim's pinyon-juniper and the bedrock canyon is from the brief (the pipeline's records), not from a source. Elevation 1360-2400 m in Arizona (FEIS). FEIS found no fire information, so disturbed 0.8 is a guess. Eaters and cover: browsed by deer, sheep and goats but not important browse, unpalatable to cattle and horses; fair cover for pronghorn, upland game birds, small birds and small mammals (FEIS); NPS names it a host of the spring azure butterfly. California quail stands in for the upland game birds (Gambel's quail is not in the library), the brush rabbit for cottontails and the deer mouse for small mammals; pronghorn, desert bighorn, Gambel's quail and the spring azure butterfly are not in the library. USDA PLANTS (its profile service) was read only for the name, growth habit (shrub) and native status. Colours, crown profile, porosity, stem count, winter leaf hold and flower size and density are the drafter's judgement, not from a source.
